name: opus-pure
workload: Opus encode and decode of generated 48 kHz speech/music test signals, 20 ms frames, complexity 9, in-process, 8 s of audio per case, fastest of 12 passes, run through SILK, hybrid and CELT modes.
claimed_speedup: Encode 1.09-1.76x faster than libopus (SILK 1.09-1.12x, e.g. 218x vs 195x realtime for SILK NB 8 kb/s mono; CELT 128 kb/s 204x vs 116x realtime = 1.76x); decode slower or at parity, 0.84-1.02x of libopus (e.g. SILK NB 3432x vs 3958x realtime).
compiler_and_flags: Rust crate at cargo default release settings, no RUSTFLAGS, no -march=native (rustc version only stated as 1.88 or newer); libopus 1.6.1 built with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, OPUS_USE_NEON=ON with runtime dispatch, float build (also a fixed-point build for a second column); C compiler not named.
stars_or_usage: 2 stars; 19+ commits; on crates.io as opus-pure
tradeoffs: Pure Rust, no C API or FFI exposed (callable from C++ only by writing a wrapper); no dependencies; hand-written NEON/SIMD kernels for CELT. Decode is not faster than libopus. Chunk-parallel encode is lossy relative to serial encode. Ogg reader seeks only to the start.
caveats: Single machine (aarch64 Apple M1 Pro); x86 results are not given. SILK encode is a fixed-point port, so the harness reports a second table against fixed-point libopus where the ratio differs. The README states hybrid is not exactly like-for-like with either libopus build. The harness (cspeed.c, rspeed, run.sh) is in the repo, which is why this is tier A; the toolchain versions are not pinned.
found_via: crates.io API searches (opus, audio codec, libopus, and others) then a raw README scan of about 1,500 audio/video crate repos for speed claims against named baselines; opened github.com/stephenberry/opus-pure, its commits page and reference/speed

name: libopus-rs
workload: 48 kHz stereo CELT-only, 5 ms (240-sample) frames, maximum complexity, 16-bit and 24-bit PCM, CBR and constrained VBR at 192/256/320 kb/s; direct in-process encode and decode of 4 x 10 s excerpts, three alternating Rust/C rounds, median per source.
claimed_speedup: Encode 1.19-2.36% less time and decode 1.50-4.64% less time than trunk libopus in all 12 aggregate cells (e.g. 16-bit CBR 192 kb/s: encode 371.9 ms vs 380.9 ms, decode 95.3 ms vs 100.0 ms per 40 s of audio); Rust encoder 96.8-107.6x realtime, decoder 338-430x realtime.
compiler_and_flags: Rust release mode, ThinLTO, one codegen unit, -C target-cpu=native; C driver (tools/raw_celt_bench.c) built with -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native and linked against static libopus.a from the trunk commit; the final timing JSON records the build-flag fields as unknown because binaries were reused; compiler versions not stated.
hardware: GCP c4-highcpu-4, Intel Xeon Platinum 8581C, process pinned to CPU 2 with taskset
tradeoffs: Incomplete codec: only 48 kHz CELT-only raw frames are supported; no SILK, hybrid or Ogg Opus. Not a drop-in replacement for libopus, no C API, and encoder packets are not byte-identical to libopus. Encoder is marked experimental. Uses a private SIMD kernel path dependency crate.
caveats: Gain is only a few percent and measured on a narrow configuration (5 ms CELT, max complexity). The test corpus (SoundKit diverse-v1) is licensed local audio and is not stored in the repo, so the run is not reproducible as-is. The repository is archived and deprecated in favour of wavey-ai/soundkit (soundkit-opus/libopus-rs) per its README; that successor was not opened. Quality was checked by SNR and ViSQOL, not listening tests.
found_via: crates.io API searches (libopus, pure rust codec, and others) then a raw README scan of audio/video crate repos; opened github.com/wavey-ai/libopus-rs, its commits page, tools folder and the 2026-08-24 performance report

name: ruopus
workload: In-process Opus encode and decode of a generated 6 s mono speech/music-like 48 kHz signal in 20 ms frames, one core, expressed as times realtime (benches/vs_libopus.rs).
claimed_speedup: Decode faster than SIMD libopus on speech: SILK wideband 16 kb/s 2095x vs 1171x realtime (1.79x), hybrid fullband 32 kb/s 1199x vs 850x (1.41x); CELT fullband 64 kb/s 1389x vs 1566x (0.89x, slower). Encode at matched complexity 0 is at parity (0.99-1.00x); against libopus default complexity 10, SILK wideband 16 kb/s encode 703x vs 221x (3.18x).
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench --bench vs_libopus --features std; release profile opt-level=3, lto=fat, codegen-units=1 (Cargo.toml); libopus 1.6.1 reached through the opus FFI crate against the system libopus, so its build flags are not stated.
hardware: one core pinned to a single performance core; CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 1 star; on crates.io as ruopus (about 6.9k downloads)
tradeoffs: Pure Rust Opus encoder and decoder with Python bindings and wasm32 support; no C API or FFI exposed, so C++ use needs a wrapper. Encoder does not yet implement delayed-decision noise-shaping quantization or warped noise shaping.
caveats: CPU model and OS not stated. The 3.18x encode figure compares a ruopus encoder with no complexity-dependent slowdown against libopus at complexity 10, so the work is not equal; at matched complexity 0 encode is at parity. CELT decode is slower than libopus. Benchmark signal is synthetic. Benchmark harness is public (benches/vs_libopus.rs) but flags of the linked libopus are unknown.
found_via: crates.io API searches (opus, audio codec) and README scan of audio/video crate repos; opened github.com/jmg049/ruopus, its commits page, Cargo.toml and benches/vs_libopus.rs

name: nanomp3
workload: In-memory MP3 decode throughput in MiB/s of MP3 input on three streams (48 kHz stereo 320 kbps, 22 kHz MPEG-2 mixed bitrates, mode switching with short blocks).
claimed_speedup: 76.0 vs 71.9 MiB/s (minimp3 SIMD) and 67.8 (scalar) on 48 kHz stereo 320 kbps; 72.7 vs 60.3 / 53.0 on 22 kHz MPEG-2 mixed bitrates; 52.6 vs 47.5 / 42.5 on mode-switching short blocks (about 1.06x to 1.21x over minimp3 SIMD, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: C reference builds compiled with clang -O3 on Windows; Rust flags and rustc version not stated; reproduce with cargo bench -p nanomp3-parity (builds upstream minimp3 from a git submodule).
hardware: Windows x86-64, CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 22 stars; 3 forks; on crates.io as nanomp3
tradeoffs: Safe Rust port of minimp3 (forbid(unsafe_code)), bit-exact with minimp3 on its conformance vectors, no_std core crate with explicit SIMD via the wide crate; fixes a few minimp3 bugs by default (opt-out via minimp3_compat). No C API, so C++ callers need a wrapper. Also decodes MP1/MP2.
caveats: Baseline minimp3 is itself a small decoder, not libmpg123 or FFmpeg, so this is a modest win over a minimp3 port target. CPU model not stated, three workloads only, and the table is first-party. Speedup over minimp3 SIMD is 6-21 percent. Comparison is Rust versus C under clang, not C++ std.
found_via: crates.io API search q=mp3 decoder (nanomp3 and nanomp3-core listed) and README scan; opened github.com/robbie01/nanomp3 and its commits page

name: NonIntegerSRC (Holters-Parker resampler)
workload: Non-integer sample-rate conversion speed of a Holters-Parker 4th-order Butterworth IIR-based SIMD resampler versus libsamplerate SRC_SINC_FASTEST for four rate pairs.
claimed_speedup: Speed factor over libsamplerate (SRC_SINC_FASTEST) from the repo's speed chart: 48k to 96k 39.8x, 96k to 48k 16.9x, 44.1k to 48k 21.2x, 48k to 44.1k 21.8x.
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build (cmake -Bbuild; cmake --build build --config Release); compiler version not stated
hardware: author's Linux machine, CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Holters-Parker resampler uses SSE-vectorised 4th-order IIR filters (from a DAFx-2018 paper) rather than a windowed-sinc FIR, so quality (aliasing and passband) differs from libsamplerate; the Lanczos resampler and SSE complex classes are borrowed from Surge Synthesizer. GPLv3 copyleft.
caveats: Numbers are only in a chart image (read from doc/speed_chart.png), with no CPU, compiler version or raw data. libsamplerate was run at its lowest-quality sinc mode, so the comparison is not quality-matched. The README text states the HP resampler is faster but gives no figures, and the 10-40x range is repeated in the author's blog (blocked, not opened). Last commit in 2021.
found_via: WebSearch: SIMD resampler faster than libsamplerate benchmark; opened github.com/jatinchowdhury18/NonIntegerSRC, its commits page and doc/speed_chart.png

name: av-denoise
workload: GPU video denoising throughput in fps on 1080p 8-bit and 4K 10-bit clips on an AMD RX9700 (NLMeans with FFmpeg default settings, NLMeans-HQ and NL4D versus FFmpeg's NLMeans OpenCL).
claimed_speedup: README text: around 2x FFmpeg's nlmeans_opencl at matched settings and about 1.3x faster than V-BM3DHIP. The 1080p CLI bar chart shows av-denoise NLMeans (FFmpeg defaults) at roughly 115 fps, NLMeans-HQ about 105 fps, NL4D about 79 fps versus FFmpeg NLMeans OpenCL about 10.5 fps (values read from the bar chart, approximate); the 4K 10-bit chart shows av-denoise at about 12.5-15.7 fps with no FFmpeg bar.
hardware: AMD RX9700 GPU (host CPU not stated)
tradeoffs: GPU-only (CubeCL kernels via ROCm, CUDA, Vulkan or Metal; no software backend); CLI, Rust library and VapourSynth plugin, no C API; kernels compile on first run (about 10 s, cached). NLMeans-HQ and NL4D are limited inside the VapourSynth plugin.
caveats: The text says about 2x at matched settings, but the chart bars suggest a larger gap against FFmpeg's default-settings baseline; the two are not reconciled on the page. No benchmark code, FFmpeg version, clip or driver stack is given on the README, and the figures are images. The FFmpeg baseline is a GPU OpenCL filter, not a CPU codec.
found_via: crates.io API searches (video/audio keywords incl. denoise, scale, pixel) with description filter for speed words, then README scan; opened github.com/ChillFish8/av-denoise, its commits page and the two benchmark chart images

name: pedalboard
baseline: pySoX (SoX command-line wrapper), SoxBindings (libsox bindings), librosa.load
workload: Python audio effect processing for single transforms and audio file reading, compared against pySoX, SoxBindings and librosa.load.
claimed_speedup: Processes audio up to 300x faster than pySoX for single transforms and 2-5x faster than SoxBindings; reads audio files up to 4x faster than librosa.load (in many cases).
tradeoffs: Python-first API on a JUCE C++ core; GPL-3.0 (copyleft, commercial licensing through JUCE terms may apply); releases the GIL so multiple cores can be used; wheels cover macOS, Windows and Linux.
caveats: The README gives no hardware, compiler, corpus or benchmark code; the SoxBindings figure is credited to a third-party repo that was not opened. The 300x figure is against pySoX, which launches a SoX subprocess per transform, so it measures process overhead more than DSP speed. Baselines are Python wrappers, not FFmpeg, libsamplerate or libopus, so this fits the video-audio category only loosely.
found_via: PyPI JSON API metadata check of audio packages (pedalboard) and its README; opened github.com/spotify/pedalboard and its commits page

name: fast-vad
baseline: webrtcvad (Google WebRTC voice activity detector, C)
workload: Voice activity detection speed on speech audio, measured relative to Silero VAD (ONNX) as the 1x baseline, with accuracy checked on AVA-Speech and LibriVAD.
claimed_speedup: Processing speed relative to Silero ONNX: fast_vad offline 721x, fast_vad streaming 129x, webrtcvad 63x; README says significantly faster than WebRTC VAD and the page says the streaming path is about 2x faster than WebRTC VAD (offline about 11.4x, derived from page data: 721/63).
stars_or_usage: 28 stars; on crates.io and PyPI as fast-vad
tradeoffs: Logistic-regression VAD on 8 log-energy bands (16 kHz and 8 kHz only, 32 ms frames); no C API (Rust and Python only); offline path uses rayon across cores. Accuracy is lower than Silero on hard audio.
caveats: Bar-chart plots only, no flags or compiler stated; the offline 721x figure uses all 16 threads while webrtcvad is a single-thread binding, so it is not per-core. On AVA-Speech fast_vad F1 is 0.680 against 0.738 (Silero) and 0.669 (webrtcvad), so the speed comes with a quality gap. A bench_rs directory is in the repo but its harness was not opened. Baseline is not in the FFmpeg, x264, Opus list.
found_via: crates.io README scan (repos from crate searches for audio keywords); opened github.com/AtharvBhat/fast-vad, docs/README.md and its commits page

name: rustrtc
workload: WebRTC peer-to-peer data-channel benchmark over a 10 s run (cargo run -r --example benchmark): throughput in MB/s, message rate, setup latency, CPU and memory, rustrtc against webrtc-rs and a pion Go program.
claimed_speedup: Throughput 549.04 MB/s vs 165.98 (webrtc-rs) and 169.58 (pion), about 3.3x and 3.2x; message rate 562,214 vs 169,967 and 173,648 msg/s; setup latency 0.45 ms vs 25.64 ms and 3.00 ms; memory 21 MB vs 44 MB and 48 MB; CPU usage 739.62% vs 677.95% and 555.20% (higher for rustrtc).
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.97.1 (2026-07-14), go 1.24.4 linux/amd64; release build via cargo run -r --example benchmark (no extra flags stated)
hardware: Intel Core i7-9700T @ 2.00GHz (8 cores), Debian 13, kernel 6.12.101
tradeoffs: Pure Rust WebRTC, RTP/SRTP, T.38 fax and UPnP stack, no C API; claims interoperability with Chrome and pion. Uses more CPU than pion in the same run.
caveats: The workload is data-channel traffic (bytes and messages), not RTP media or codec processing, so category fit is weak and the baselines (webrtc-rs, pion) are not C or C++ and not in the FFmpeg/x264/Opus list; libwebrtc was not compared. The numbers are the author's own run on one 2019 laptop-class CPU, reproduced with the in-repo example (examples/benchmark.rs, which builds the Go comparison itself).
found_via: crates.io API search q=video codec (rustrtc listed: high-performance WebRTC, RTP/SRTP) and README scan; opened github.com/restsend/rustrtc, its commits page and examples/benchmark.rs
